questions.prompt: The small-signal conductance of a forward-biased diode at bias current \(I_D\) is
questions.explanation: \(g_d=\dfrac{dI_D}{dV_D}=\dfrac{qI_D}{kT}\) (reader Eq. 6.28): the slope of the exponential is proportional to the current itself. \(I_D/V_D\) is the large-signal ratio, a different (much smaller) number. \(V_t/I_D\) is \(r_d\), the reciprocal.

questions.prompt: The diode small-signal model is valid when the signal voltage \(v_d\) satisfies
options: Any amplitude, as long as the diode is forward-biased
questions.explanation: Linearizing \(e^{v_d/V_t}\approx1+v_d/V_t\) requires \(v_d/V_t\ll1\) (reader Sec. 6.6). Even 10 mV gives a noticeable error. The relevant scale is \(V_t\), not the bias voltage.

questions.prompt: A diode with transit time \(\tau_F=2\ \mathrm{ns}\) is biased at 1 mA. What is its diffusion capacitance \(C_{diff}=\tau_F\dfrac{I_D}{V_t}\), in pF?
questions.explanation: \(C_{diff}=\tau_Fg_d=2\times10^{-9}\times\dfrac{10^{-3}}{0.0259}=77.22\ \mathrm{pF}\) (reader Eq. 6.33). It comes from stored minority charge \(Q_s=I_D\tau_F\).

questions.prompt: For that diode (\(C_{diff}=77.2\ \mathrm{pF}\)), \(C_{j0}=1\ \mathrm{pF}\). Using the reader's forward-bias estimate \(C_j\approx1.4C_{j0}\), what is the total small-signal capacitance, in pF?
questions.explanation:
The two capacitances are in parallel (Fig. 6.14): \(C_{tot}=C_j+C_{diff}=1.4+77.2=78.62\ \mathrm{pF}\).
In forward bias at mA currents the diffusion capacitance dominates.

questions.prompt: Which capacitance dominates the diode's small-signal model in strong forward bias, and which in reverse bias?
options: Forward: diffusion capacitance (grows with \(I_D\)); reverse: junction (depletion) capacitance, since \(C_{diff}\approx0\)
questions.explanation: \(C_{diff}=\tau_FI_D/V_t\) is proportional to current, large in forward bias and negligible when \(I_D\approx-I_S\). \(C_j\) exists in both regions but is only a few pF; in reverse bias it's all that's left (and \(g_d\approx0\)).

questions.prompt: A diode is biased at \(I_D\) and a \(+10\ \mathrm{mV}\) step is applied. The exact current change is \(I_D(e^{v/V_t}-1)\); the small-signal estimate is \(g_dv\). By what percentage does the exact change exceed the estimate (\(V_t=25.9\ \mathrm{mV}\))?
questions.explanation:
\(x=10/25.9=0.386\). Exact/linear \(=\dfrac{e^{x}-1}{x}=\dfrac{0.4712}{0.386}=1.2203\), so the estimate is 22.05% low.
Gotcha: 10 mV is not ≪ 26 mV. For a 1% error you need \(|v|\lesssim0.5\ \mathrm{mV}\).

questions.prompt: Two diodes, one with 10× the area (10× \(I_S\)) of the other, are both biased at 1 mA. How do their small-signal resistances compare?
options: They are equal (\(r_d=V_t/I_D=25.9\ \Omega\)); the larger diode just needs a lower \(V_D\)
questions.explanation: \(g_d=I_D/V_t\) contains no \(I_S\): at a given CURRENT the slope of an exponential is the same. Area only shifts the curve in voltage by \(V_t\ln10=60\ \mathrm{mV}\). (Its junction capacitance is larger, though.)

questions.prompt: What is the small-signal model of a diode reverse-biased at \(-3\ \mathrm{V}\)?
options: Essentially just the junction capacitance \(C_j(-3\ \mathrm{V})\); \(g_d\approx0\) and \(C_{diff}\approx0\)
questions.explanation: With \(I_D\approx-I_S\), \(g_d=\dfrac{dI}{dV}=\dfrac{I_Se^{V/V_t}}{V_t}\approx0\) and no minority charge is stored, so \(C_{diff}\approx0\). What's left is the depletion capacitance, which is how varactors are used. (\(I_S/V_t\) would be the conductance at zero bias, not at \(-3\ \mathrm{V}\).)

questions.prompt: Preview of the BJT small-signal model. A BJT's collector current \(I_C=I_Se^{V_{BE}/V_t}\) has transconductance \(g_m=dI_C/dV_{BE}\). At \(I_C=1\ \mathrm{mA}\), what is \(g_m\), in mS?
questions.explanation: Same derivative as the diode: \(g_m=I_C/V_t=1\ \mathrm{mA}/25.9\ \mathrm{mV}=38.6\ \mathrm{mS}\). The BJT small-signal model starts from the diode's \(g_d\).

questions.prompt: Preview of \(f_T\). When \(C_{diff}\) dominates, the diode's \(g_d\) and \(C_{diff}=\tau_Fg_d\) set a corner frequency \(\dfrac{g_d}{2\pi C_{diff}}\). For \(\tau_F=50\ \mathrm{ps}\), what is it, in GHz?
questions.explanation:
\(\dfrac{g_d}{2\pi\tau_Fg_d}=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\tau_F}=\dfrac{1}{2\pi\times50\times10^{-12}}=3.183\ \mathrm{GHz}\), independent of the current.
Transistors have an analogous speed limit, their unity-gain frequency \(f_T\).

questions.prompt: Preview of small-signal analysis. A diode is biased at 1 mA through \(R=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) from a DC source, and a small AC signal is added to that source. What fraction of the AC signal appears across the diode?
options: About 70%, since the diode drops 0.7 V
0%, since the DC source shorts AC
questions.explanation:
For small signals, replace the DC source by a short (its AC part remains), and the diode by \(r_d=V_t/I_D=25.9\ \Omega\). Then it's a divider: \(\dfrac{25.9}{1025.9}=2.52\%\).
This 'DC bias, then linear small-signal circuit' recipe is the core of the small-signal-model skills.
